{{Short description|In survey methodology}}
<!-- Note: The following pages were redirects to [[Probability-proportional-to-size_sampling]] before draftification:

In [[survey methodology]], '''probability-proportional-to-size (pps) sampling''' is a [[sampling (statistics)|sampling]] process where each element of the [[statistical population|population]] (of size ''N'') has some ([[statistical independence|independent]]) chance <math>p_i</math> to be selected to the sample when performing one draw. This <math>p_i</math> is proportional to some known quantity <math>x_i</math> so that <math>p_i = \frac{x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^N x_i}</math>.<ref name="sarndal1992">{{cite book
 |title = Model Assisted Survey Sampling
 |author=Carl-Erik Sarndal |author2=Bengt Swensson |author3=Jan Wretman
 |isbn= 978-0-387-97528-3
 |year = 1992
|publisher=Springer }}</ref>{{rp|97}}<ref>{{cite book |last1=Skinner |first1=Chris J. |title=Wiley StatsRef: Statistics Reference Online |chapter=Probability Proportional to Size (PPS) Sampling |date=2016 |pages=1–5 |doi=10.1002/9781118445112.stat03346.pub2 |isbn=978-1-118-44511-2 }}</ref>

One of the cases this occurs in, as developed by Hanson and Hurwitz in 1943,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hansen |first1=Morris H. |last2=Hurwitz |first2=William N. |title=On the Theory of Sampling from Finite Populations |journal=The Annals of Mathematical Statistics |date=1943 |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=333–362 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177731356 |jstor=2235923 }}</ref> is when we have several clusters of units, each with a different (known upfront) number of units, then each cluster can be selected with a probability that is proportional to the number of units inside it.<ref name = "Cochran1977">Cochran, W. G. (1977). Sampling Techniques (3rd ed.). Nashville, TN: John Wiley & Sons. {{ISBN|978-0-471-16240-7}}</ref>{{rp|250}} So, for example, if we have 3 clusters with 10, 20 and 30 units each, then the chance of selecting the first cluster will be 1/6, the second would be 1/3, and the third cluster will be 1/2.

The pps sampling results in a fixed sample size ''n'' (as opposed to [[Poisson sampling]] which is similar but results in a random sample size with [[Expected value|expectancy]] of&nbsp;''n''). When selecting items with replacement the selection procedure is to just draw one item at a time (like getting ''n'' draws from a [[multinomial distribution]] with ''N'' elements, each with their own <math>p_i</math> selection probability). If doing a without-replacement sampling, the schema can become more complex.<ref name="sarndal1992" />{{rp|93}}

Another sampling method, [[Reservoir sampling]], is 'Weighted random sampling with a reservoir', which offers an algorithm for drawing a weighted random sample of size m from a population of n weighted items, where m⩽n, in one-pass over unknown population size.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Efraimidis |first1=Pavlos S. |last2=Spirakis |first2=Paul G. |title=Weighted random sampling with a reservoir |journal=Information Processing Letters |date=March 2006 |volume=97 |issue=5 |pages=181–185 |doi=10.1016/j.ipl.2005.11.003 }}</ref>

==Distribution and properties==

If observations from some distribution F are sampled in a way that is proportional to their value, then the distribution of the values in that sample follows a [[Length-biased distribution]], with the following density function:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mustafa |first1=Abdelfattah |last2=Khan |first2=M. I. |title=The length-biased power hazard rate distribution: Some properties and applications |journal=Statistics in Transition |series=New Series |date=June 2022 |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=1–16 |doi=10.2478/stattrans-2022-0013 |hdl=10419/266304 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>{{rp|2}}<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Kyeongjun |title=Estimation of length biased exponential distribution based on progressive hybrid censoring |journal=Communications for Statistical Applications and Methods |date=30 November 2024 |volume=31 |issue=6 |pages=661–675 |doi=10.29220/CSAM.2024.31.6.661 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

<math>g(x) = x f(x) / E[x] </math>

Also: <math>E[g(x)] = E[x^2] / E[x] </math>

Notice that this would assume that the PPS sampling is done with replacement (or if the sample size is much smaller than the population size).
